data.title: Spišský Štvrtok – the Slovak Mycenae of the Bronze Age
data.excerpt: On Myšia Hôrka at Spišský Štvrtok, people of the Otomani culture built a fortified small town some 3,500 years ago which guarded the so-called Northern Route. Gold and bronze jewellery, faience beads then known only from Egypt and work in bone and amber with Mycenaean ornament earned the site its comparison with Greek Mycenae.
data.metaTitle: Spišský Štvrtok – the Bronze Age Slovak Mycenae
data.metaDescription: Myšia Hôrka at Spišský Štvrtok, a fortress 3,500 years old on the Northern Route, nicknamed the Slovak Mycenae for its likeness to Greek Mycenae.

keyFacts.label: Area of the fortified enclosure
keyFacts.value: approximately 6,600 m², with thirty-nine houses and a cult place

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: a stone rampart 6 m wide, an outlying stone wall and a ditch 6 m wide, the main gateway in the shape of a U

keyFacts.label: Culture
keyFacts.value: the Otomani culture (Otomani-Füzesabony), the transition between the Early and the Middle Bronze Age

keyFacts.label: Important finds
keyFacts.value: gold and bronze jewellery, faience beads (until then known only from Egypt), work in bone and amber with Mycenaean ornament

children.text: For a very long time it was not known that the territory of present-day Slovakia too had a small town some 3,500 years old which had much in common with Greek Mycenae. It is Spišský Štvrtok, and specifically Myšia Hôrka, where its inhabitants of the time built a fortress at an important strategic point on the so-called Northern Route, which they guarded and controlled. Historians have named this area the Spiš Mycenae…

Probably already at this time two important routes existed in the territory of present-day Slovakia, which from the Neolithic onwards were also trade routes. The first, called the Amber Road, led from the Mediterranean along the Danube and the Morava to the north. The second led from the north-eastern Baltic along the Vistula and the Poprad, through a narrow valley past Myšia Hôrka, into the valley of the Tisza region and then on to the Balkans and the Mediterranean Sea. This eastern route, called the Northern Route, influenced the rise and the development of the fortress. Goods were transported along this busy route probably in caravan fashion from one station to the next. There were certainly also merchants who travelled the whole of this route, but they had to be able to change or to hire their means of transport, that is to say horses. A kind of fortified refreshment station served them for this purpose.

The first report of the historical fortress on Myšia Hôrka appeared only at the end of the 19th century. It was written by the archaeologist Alexander Münich, regarded as the father of the Spiš archaeologists and local-history enthusiasts. At that time remains of walls some two metres high still survived, which the local inhabitants later dismantled and used to build their houses damaged by fire. Myšia Hôrka was threatened with complete devastation, which the authorities prevented after the First World War.

During the 1960s the site was also brought to attention by František Javorský, an archaeologist and a native of Spišský Štvrtok. More than twenty years after this notice, staff of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra took up the matter and began excavation, but success was long in coming. The director of this excavation, doc. PhDr. Jozef Vlaďar, DrSc., did not give up, however, and the excavation was finally crowned with magnificent finds. He published many articles and photographs about them. Specialists assessed these finds as a European discovery.
Above all because it changed the ideas held until then about the occupation of the northern part of present-day Slovakia in the prehistoric period.

It is held that in central Europe 3,500 years ago there was prehistory and a primitive communal society, while in the south of Europe, including Greek Mycenae, a developed slave-owning society already existed. Mycenaean, Cretan and Greek cultural influences then spread from other centres of civilisation in Europe. The manner of building palaces, stone architecture and town planning, with all the Aegean currents, spread northwards along the Northern Route as well and reached Myšia Hôrka too. There must therefore have been contacts between Greek Mycenae and Myšia Hôrka, which were reflected in both material and spiritual culture, as is attested by rich finds and by objects of strategic importance.

The excavated artefacts showed that the small town on Myšia Hôrka had a perfect military fortification and houses arranged in streets according to a carefully thought-out town plan. It had an area of approximately 6,600 m² and was protected in the usual manner. The rampart protected by stone walls was 6 m wide, and in front of it there was also a separate stone wall and a ditch 6 m wide. The town, with its stone walls in the shape of the letter U, was entered through the main gateway. It also turned out that the small town had been built on the foundations of an earlier but smaller settlement, which the new builders demolished so that they could erect a more extensive and more splendid settlement.

children.text: The archaeologists came to the conclusion that the ancient settlement was built by the people of the Otomani culture, that is, by incomers from Transylvania who knew the local towns and their defences well. They were also attracted here by the rich raw-material base. The occurrence of a large quantity of copper was one of the conditions that made the rise of such a small town possible as early as the Bronze Age. This is borne out by the strikingly conspicuous similarity of the finds from Myšia Hôrka to the finds of the so-called Otomani culture, whose centre was Transylvania (Romania).

The small town on Myšia Hôrka was built on a raised site where, on one side, a steep and wooded slope falls away into the valley of the Machalovský stream. Opposite the steep slope rises a hill called Hradisko, where archaeological excavation is being carried out. The streets with their houses were laid out from the entrance gateway with its two towers and the fortification. In this it resembles the settlement uncovered at Barca near Košice. Two kinds of building were erected on Myšia Hôrka. Some belonged to the privileged stratum of the powerful, the others, outside the square, to craftsmen, merchants and soldiers. In the middle of the stone-paved square an acropolis was built, in which the privileged inhabitants resided. Their houses differed above all in the composition of the objects that were found in them. The most powerful group of people decided on the organisation of life in the small town, on trade, on the guarding of the Northern Route and certainly also on the economy of the whole region. In their houses gold and bronze jewellery was found, stored in vessels on shelves or in strong-boxes beneath the floor. The splendour of many of the objects was heightened by work in bone and amber with Mycenaean ornament. Faience beads, known at that time only in Egypt, were also found here. In the houses of the craftsmen and merchants there were found: stone products, pottery, bronze objects, moulds for casting bronze daggers and jewellery, loom weights and various ornamental objects.

children.text: It is interesting that no agricultural implements were found in the small town, which probably proves that its inhabitants evidently obtained their food supplies by exchange from the people of the wider surroundings.

The most striking feature was a sacrificial site, where human remains were also found, thrown into a pit together with various offerings. Some of the skeletons were not complete; their arms and legs were missing. Ritual mutilation was also established, a positively bestial disfigurement of the bodies, not excluding the heads of the victims. In three cases holes were also found in the back of the skull. This discovery is more than surprising, since the people who are supposed to have lived here were of a high social standing…
